extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, policymakers, and general readers interested in media/propaganda
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and describing 'pink-slime journalism' — outlets that publish low-quality, outsourced, or automated reports presented as independent local news, often with hidden partisan agendas. Useful for media analysts, journalists, and the public assessing the trustworthiness and provenance of local news sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-quality outsourced reports masquerading as local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice in which news outlets ... publish (often but not always) lower-quality news reports that appear to be independent local news outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reports are either computer-generated or written by poorly-paid outsourced writers, sometimes using pen names. This is the core definitional trait: content looks like local reporting but is low-quality and not genuinely local.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated or AI-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is generated by computer automation or AI from various datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pink-slime journalism typically involves using computer automation or AI to generate news stories; sites can be identified by heavy use of automatically generated content and templated stories. Examples: high proportion of computer-generated articles; Nieman Lab reporting on 'AI reporters'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsourcing to low-wage writers and use of pen names
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is produced by low-wage employees and writers who may not be local to the area they purport to cover, sometimes using pen names or false bylines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported pay ranges historically from $0.35 to $36 per article; examples include Journatic hiring poorly-paid non-local writers writing under fake names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy use of templates and list-like information without analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy use of templates; might just list information without any analysis or context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poynter cites templated output and lack of original reporting or contextual analysis as identifiers; templated stories often lack sourcing and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimics local/hyperlocal news design and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and naming of publications often resemble that of independent local news outlets to take advantage of trust placed in local journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites mimic local outlets' look/branding to exploit readers' faith in local news; researcher Priyanjana Bengani and Columbia Journalism Review discuss this tactic and its role in filling news deserts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part of partisan-funded networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets are part of networks financed by partisans to push their narrative or point-of-view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks may be funded by political operatives, PACs, or wealthy donors (e.g., Brian Timpone networks, Metric Media). Being part of a larger network is a signal of possible coordinated partisan aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden or undisclosed funding and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites typically do not disclose that they are funded by advocacy groups or that they are paid to run articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of transparency about funding and publisher agenda is cited repeatedly (New York Times, NewsGuard, ProPublica). Hidden funding may be revealed by investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan slant in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Present candidates and policies favored by the partisans who fund the website in a favorable light, while presenting disfavored candidates and policies negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and media credibility raters have observed partisan-backed slant across both right- and left-leaning examples; content selection and framing reflect funders' interests rather than neutral reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased production around election cycles and political targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Pink-slime websites often step up their content production during election cycles and have been used to gather data for political targeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CJR and other outlets report higher activity near elections; Columbia Journalism Review and NewsGuard note use of sites to collect user data for targeting ads and persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of original reporting; repurposed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites often repurpose content from other reports rather than produce original journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columbia Journalism Review and other research found many articles repurposed; reports note >90% of some networks' output was computer-generated or repurposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive bylines and fabricated quotes/plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of false bylines, fabricated quotes, and plagiarized material have been documented in pink-slime operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journatic exposé revealed false bylines, fabricated quotes, and plagiarism; such practices triggered contract cancellations by mainstream newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not necessarily false but rooted in deception (lack of fairness/transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites do not typically post false information, but the operation is rooted in deception, eschewing hallmarks of news reporting like fairness and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York Times characterization: deceptive practices may be subtle (omitting disclosures, slanted framing) rather than outright falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large scale and network footprint as an indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of many sites tied to an operator or network (hundreds to >1,000 sites) indicates organized pink-slime operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research found networks (e.g., Metric Media, Locality Labs, Record Inc.) creating dozens or hundreds of local sites quickly; scale itself can be a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running ads and hiding partisan funding/connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms running ads on social media while hiding their partisan funding and connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NewsGuard and other investigations reported sites running advertising campaigns while concealing partisan backers; look for missing funding disclosures on ads and sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use to gather user data
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of these websites to gather user data has been observed, sometimes for political targeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports indicate data-collection practices tied to broader political ad targeting strategies; combined with deceptive presentation this raises ethical and political concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: High quantity of sites and rapid expansion into news deserts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid increase in number of such sites, often filling voids left by shuttered local newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CJR and others documented hundreds to thousands of sites appearing in local news deserts; growth patterns—especially sudden spikes—are notable indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of relatively high-quality work that conceals non-journalistic agenda ('news mirage')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some websites produce relatively high-quality work but obscure the non-journalistic agenda of their publisher, serving as mouthpieces for corporations or advocacy groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'news mirage' (coined 2024) flags outlets that look like legitimate newsrooms but function primarily as advocacy or corporate mouthpieces; high production quality does not guarantee independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic indicator: extremely low pay for content producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers employed by pink-slime networks historically received very low pay per article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented pay ranges (e.g., $0.35–$24 in 2012; $3–$36 reported in 2020) indicate business models cut labor costs, which correlates with lower-quality reporting and outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication of conservational or partisan talking points rather than local reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Many distributed articles reflect partisan talking points or nationalized content rather than genuine local reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CJR found many articles across networks pushed conservative talking points; look for repeated templates/messages across supposedly local outlets.
